plants.name: Jacaranda mimosifolia
plants.description: A fast-growing tree with fern-like leaves that erupts into dense clusters of trumpet-shaped lavender-blue flowers, often carpeting streets and lawns with fallen petals.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late spring to early summer in the Southern Hemisphere (October to December)
plants.location: Native to South America; widely planted in Australia, South Africa (Pretoria), and Argentina
plants.funFact: In Pretoria, South Africa, jacarandas line the streets in such numbers that the city is nicknamed 'Jacaranda City', and a fallen blossom on your head is said to bring good luck.

plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: A bulbous perennial whose crocus-like pink-lilac flowers emerge from bare ground in autumn, with leaves appearing only the following spring.
plants.location: Meadows and woodland edges across Europe; cultivated in gardens in temperate regions worldwide
plants.funFact: All parts of the plant contain colchicine, a toxic alkaloid that is also used in medicine to treat gout and in plant breeding to induce chromosome doubling.

plants.name: Aster novae-angliae
plants.description: A tall, hardy perennial wildflower with sturdy hairy stems topped with masses of daisy-like flowers featuring golden-yellow centers and many narrow petals.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer to mid-autumn (August to October)
plants.location: Eastern and central North America in prairies, meadows, and roadsides
plants.funFact: It is a crucial late-season nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies, which fuel up on its flowers during their journey to Mexico.

plants.name: Camellia sasanqua
plants.description: An evergreen shrub with glossy dark leaves and delicate, often fragrant flowers that open earlier than most other camellias, brightening autumn gardens.
plants.bloomingSeason: Autumn to early winter (October to December)
plants.location: Native to Japan; cultivated in the southeastern United States, Europe, and Australia
plants.funFact: It is a close relative of Camellia sinensis, the plant that gives us tea, and its seeds are pressed to produce camellia oil used in cooking and cosmetics.
